title: Contingency planning
blurb: Separate fallback plans from contingency reserves and management reserve, and explain how contingency is sized and controlled.
question: A data centre migration team agrees that if the new servers fail testing, the company will keep running on the old servers for an extra month. It also sets aside money to pay for the extended lease. Which part is the fallback plan, which is the contingency, and who should control spending it?

teach.h: Plan B, and the time and money to pay for it
teach.body: CONTINGENCY PLANNING means deciding in advance what you will do if a risk occurs (a FALLBACK PLAN) and reserving time or money (CONTINGENCY) to deal with risks that may occur. Contingency is then controlled and drawn down through governance, not spent at will. Plain English: you don't wait for the storm to decide where the umbrellas are, or how you'll pay for them.

teach.caption: A fallback plan says WHAT you'll do. Contingency is the time or money that pays for it.

teach.h: Fallback plans: reactive, but planned early
teach.body: A fallback plan is a REACTIVE response: it is used only after a risk occurs, or if the main response fails. Its value comes from being worked out BEFORE it is needed, with a clear TRIGGER (the point at which you switch to it), an owner and any resources reserved. Deciding under pressure, mid-crisis, produces slower and costlier choices. Fallbacks are usually written for the higher-priority threats, where the impact would hurt most.

teach.h: How the project budget is built up
teach.caption: Contingency is controlled by the PM and sponsor according to delegated tolerances. Management reserve is held by the sponsor or board.

teach.body: Contingency should come from the RISK ANALYSIS, not a habitual flat percentage. For each identified risk, the team considers how likely it is and what it would cost in time or money, and the contingency reflects that exposure. Too little, and the first threat that lands forces an escalation or a cut. Too much, and money is tied up that could fund other work, and teams may relax their control. Realistic contingency is one of the benefits of risk management.

teach.caption: The school must open for the new term, so time contingency protects the handover milestone. Drawing on it needs approval, like money.

steps.label: Request
steps.sub: PM requests draw-down, linked to the risk

steps.label: Approve
steps.sub: Within PM tolerance, or by the sponsor

teach.caption: When a risk passes without occurring, its contingency can be released too, again through governance.

teach.text: Three classic confusions. (1) A fallback plan is a PLAN; contingency is TIME OR MONEY. (2) Contingency covers IDENTIFIED risks; management reserve covers UNKNOWNS and is held by the sponsor or board, not the PM. (3) Contingency is not a pot for new scope or poor estimating: extra scope goes through change control.

teach.h: Contingency in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: Fixed
values: Time and cost per time box

teach.caption: In iterative delivery the deadline doesn't move, so lower-priority (e.g. Could have) items act as the contingency.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define contingency planning: deciding responses in advance and reserving time or cost for risks.
Distinguish a fallback plan (a reactive plan with a trigger) from contingency (time or money).
Explain sizing: from analysed risk exposure, not a guess.
Explain control: drawn down through governance within tolerances; management reserve held higher.
Note the life cycle: reserves in linear, flexible scope in iterative.
Contingency planning = fallback plans decided in advance + time or cost reserved for risks.
Fallback plan: reactive, used if the risk occurs (or the main response fails), with a trigger and owner.
Contingency: for identified risks, sized from risk analysis, drawn down via approval.
Management reserve: for unknowns, held by the sponsor or board.
Unused contingency is released through governance; it never funds new scope.

summary: You can now explain contingency planning, tell a fallback plan from a contingency reserve and from management reserve, and describe how contingency is sized and controlled. You can also explain why iterative projects hold their contingency mainly in flexible scope.

A.q: Which of the following best describes a fallback plan?
options: Money set aside for unknown risks
A planned action used if a risk occurs
A plan to stop a risk from ever arising
A record of risks closed at the end
A.why: A fallback plan is a reactive response, worked out in advance and put into action if the risk occurs.

whyNot.0: Money for unknown risks is management reserve, not a plan of action.
whyNot.2: Stopping a risk arising is a proactive response such as avoidance, not a fallback.
whyNot.3: Closed risks are recorded in the register; that isn't a fallback plan.

A.q: A project's contingency budget is primarily intended to cover…
options: new scope requested by users
unknown, unforeseeable events
overspends from poor estimating
the impact of identified risks
A.why: Contingency is time or money reserved for identified (known) risks, sized from the risk analysis.

whyNot.0: New scope goes through change control and needs its own funding decision.
whyNot.1: Unknown events are covered by management reserve, held by the sponsor or board.
whyNot.2: Contingency isn't a pot to absorb poor estimating; estimates should be corrected and reported.

A.q: Which is the best basis for deciding how much contingency a project needs?
options: The analysed exposure of its risks
A flat percentage used every time
Whatever the sponsor has spare
The amount the last project used
A.why: Contingency should reflect the probability and impact of the project's own identified risks.

whyNot.1: A habitual percentage ignores this project's actual risks.
whyNot.2: Spare money is not a measure of risk exposure.
whyNot.3: Every project is unique; another project's figure doesn't reflect these risks.

B.q: On a museum refurbishment, the project manager uses contingency to add an extra gallery the director has just asked for. What is the main problem?
options: Contingency may only be spent on time
Galleries must be funded by the board
Contingency is for risks, not new scope
The director cannot request any change
B.why: New scope must go through change control. Using contingency for it hides the change and leaves the identified risks unfunded.

whyNot.0: Contingency can be time or money; the problem is what it's being used for.
whyNot.1: The issue isn't who funds galleries, it's bypassing change control.
whyNot.3: Stakeholders can request changes; they must be assessed through change control.

B.q: Which statement about fallback plans and contingency is correct?
options: A fallback plan replaces the need for contingency
Contingency is only agreed after a risk occurs
A fallback plan is used only if a risk happens
Management reserve is held by the PM alone
B.why: A fallback plan is reactive: it is prepared in advance but only put into action if the risk occurs (or the main response fails).

whyNot.0: They work together: the fallback says what to do, contingency pays for it.
whyNot.1: Contingency is sized and reserved in advance, then drawn down when needed.
whyNot.3: Management reserve is held by the sponsor or board, not the PM.

B.q: In an iterative project where time and cost are fixed for each time box, where is contingency mainly held?
options: In extra time added to each time box
In lower-priority scope that can drop
In a reserve held by the main supplier
In a larger team kept on permanent standby
B.why: Because the deadline and budget don't move, lower-priority items (such as Could haves) are dropped if needed: scope is the contingency.

whyNot.0: Time boxes have fixed end dates; extending them defeats the approach.
whyNot.2: Suppliers don't hold the project's contingency.
whyNot.3: A standby team would add cost; iterative delivery flexes scope instead.

C.q: A bridge project set aside contingency for the risk of a winter flood delaying piling. Spring arrives, piling is complete and the risk has passed. What should happen to that contingency?
options: Kept by the PM for any future overspend
Spent on extra features while it's there
Left untouched until the final close-down
Released or reallocated via governance
C.why: When a risk passes, its contingency is no longer needed for it. Releasing or reallocating it is a governance decision, keeping the budget transparent.

whyNot.0: Contingency isn't a general fund for overspends; using it that way hides problems.
whyNot.1: New features are new scope and need change control.
whyNot.2: Leaving it idle ties up money; it should be released through governance once the risk has gone.

C.q: Why should contingency draw-down be controlled through governance? 1. To keep spending visible against specific risks. 2. To stop it being used for scope creep. 3. To excuse the PM from reporting on budget. 4. To ensure decisions are made at the right level. Select the correct combination.
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 3 and 4
C.why: Controlled draw-down keeps spend transparent (1), protects it from scope creep (2) and puts each decision with the right authority (4).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is wrong: governance increases, not removes, the need for budget reporting.
whyNot.2: Statement 3 is wrong, and 1 (visibility) is a key reason.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is wrong, and 2 (preventing scope creep) is a key reason.

C.q: A data migration team agrees that if the new servers fail testing, the business will stay on the old servers for another month, and it sets aside money to pay for the extended lease. How are these two elements best described?
options: A fallback plan and a contingency
A reduce response and a reserve
A transfer response and a change
An avoid response and a baseline
C.why: Staying on the old servers is a reactive plan if the risk occurs (fallback); the money reserved for the lease is contingency.

whyNot.1: Nothing here lowers the probability or impact in advance, and the money is for an identified risk, not unknowns.
whyNot.2: No risk is passed to a third party, and nothing is changing the baseline.
whyNot.3: The risk is not being removed, and money set aside isn't a baseline.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: A family is refitting their kitchen on a tight budget. How do fallback plans, contingency and a 'just in case' reserve show up in their plans?

blocks.body: The worktop might be delivered late. Their FALLBACK PLAN: fit a cheap temporary board so the sink can go in, then swap it later. Old houses often hide damp behind units, so they keep £800 of CONTINGENCY for that identified risk. And they leave some savings untouched for anything nobody has thought of: that is like MANAGEMENT RESERVE, and only the joint decision of both parents can unlock it.

head: Safety net
Covers
Who can use it
rows: The fitter, if the date slips

blocks.text: If the family spends the damp fund on a fancier tap, there's nothing left if the damp appears. That is why contingency is for risks, not for new wants.

explain.body: A reactive plan, decided in advance, put into action if a risk occurs or the main response fails. It needs a clear trigger, an owner and any resources reserved beforehand.

test.q: What usually prompts a team to put its fallback plan into action?
options: The start of each new project phase
A request from any stakeholder
The risk occurs or its trigger is hit
The risk owner going on annual leave
test.why: Fallback plans are reactive: they are triggered when the risk occurs, or when an agreed trigger point is reached.

whyNot.0: Phase changes are review points, not triggers for a fallback.
whyNot.1: Fallbacks are tied to the risk, not to ad hoc stakeholder requests.
whyNot.3: Staff absence doesn't trigger a risk's fallback; the risk occurring does.

explain.body: Contingency: time or money for IDENTIFIED risks, controlled by the PM and sponsor according to delegated tolerances. Management reserve: money for UNKNOWN risks, held by the sponsor or board.

test.q: A risk nobody had foreseen hits a museum project. Which reserve is designed for this, and who typically holds it?
options: Contingency, held by the risk owner
Management reserve, held by the sponsor
Contingency, held by the main supplier
Fallback reserve, held by the PMO
test.why: Unforeseen (unknown) risks are covered by management reserve, held by the sponsor or board.

whyNot.0: Contingency covers identified risks, and risk owners don't hold the budget reserve.
whyNot.2: Suppliers don't hold the client's reserves, and this risk wasn't identified.
whyNot.3: There is no 'fallback reserve'; a fallback is a plan, and the PMO doesn't hold reserves.

explain.body: Each draw-down is requested against a specific risk, approved at the right level (within the PM's tolerance, or by the sponsor above it), recorded, and reflected in the register, budget and forecast.

test.q: A project manager needs more contingency than their delegated tolerance allows. What should they do?
options: Spend it now and report it later
Take it from management reserve
Split it into smaller requests
Seek approval from the sponsor
test.why: Beyond delegated tolerance, the decision must be escalated to the sponsor (or above).

whyNot.1: Management reserve is held by the sponsor or board; the PM can't take it.
whyNot.2: Splitting a request to dodge a limit undermines the tolerance.

explain.body: Linear: contingency is held as time and cost reserves, often as buffers before milestones, approved by tolerance at gates. Iterative: time and cost per time box are fixed, so flexible lower-priority scope is the contingency.

test.q: A council's digital team works in fixed four-week time boxes. Midway through one, a key integration takes longer than expected. Using its contingency, what does the team most likely do?
options: Drop a lower-priority item this time box
Extend this time box by two more weeks
Ask the sponsor for management reserve
Raise a fallback plan for the whole release
test.why: In iterative delivery the time box end is fixed; lower-priority scope is dropped or deferred to protect it.

whyNot.1: Extending the time box breaks the fixed time that the approach depends on.
whyNot.2: Management reserve is for unknowns at a higher level, not routine overruns in a time box.
whyNot.3: A fallback plan responds to a specific identified risk; flexing scope is the normal mechanism here.
